newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: War, Afghan style, rolls on.
newsitem.headline: War, Afghan style, rolls on.

text.p: The road north of Kabul is empty except for pick-ups crammed with Taleban fighters, the occasional tank and a refugee family or two, walking deliberately under a stormy sky.

After a fortnight's relative peace, Afghanistan's wearying civil war has come again to the villages and towns on this dusty plain, as the country's new Islamic Taleban government faces forces loyal to former military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
The road, usually a noisy bustle of trucks, taxis and buses laden with passengers and produce, is eerily empty.
Young Taleban fighters at a checkpoint show little interest in passing traffic.
Ahead, as the road stretches into the last plain before the Hindu Kush mountains, distant mud-brick villages and lines of nomads' tents offer little contrast to the brown landscape.
Pick-ups and the odd car -- one a Mercedes -- race by, overtaking tanks that rattle along past deserted houses. All carry the Taleban's makeshift white flag symbolising purity.
To one side of the road, nomads load their possessions into trucks. From a village a small column of refugees walks alongside the road, pleading for a lift to Kabul.
"A few shells landed near our house this morning, and so my children persuaded me to leave," said 35-year old Faizal, carrying a single bag over his shoulder.

He left behind some brothers to look after the house but was clearly anxious. His family, the women all in full-length veils ordered by the Taleban, keep walking another 100 metres (yards) on, then crouch by the side of the road.
A young boy, sporting a bright pink waistcoat, plays with a lame dog apparently abandoned earlier during the exodus.
"I have left everything behind. We really believed (after the Taleban takeover) we would have some peace," Faizal says.

Further on lie deserted villages where newer houses are bunched next to the bombed-out hulks of older ones destroyed when Soviet forces tried to hold control of the road against the marauding mujahideen in the 1980s.
Now it appears to be the Taleban's turn, as fighters loyal to the ousted government launch guerrilla attacks on the road, Taleban guardposts and a nearby military airbase.

Taleban jeeps, tanks and rocket launchers gather at one village but few of their crew seem to know what is going on further up the road. "It's not good to wait here. We could be a target," advised one young soldier.

Ahead, in a ditch by the roadside, a large Taleban fighter is loading a jeep-mounted rocket launcher, casually walking a few metres (yards) before a deafening roar sends the rockets hurtling towards a village at the base of the mountains.
Fighters perched on a nearby mound watch as plumes of smoke and dust indicate where the rockets landed.
No one seems too sure what the target is.
"Fire anywhere. Don't care about the civilians," one Taleban, limping from a foot wound, yells.
A loudspeaker across the road plays the Moslem call to prayer but the purist Islamic Taleban do not seem to notice.
They turn their gaze to the east, where rocket launchers and tanks further up the road aim at positions nn distant peaks.

Lightning splits darkening rain clouds over the western mountain range. Further along can be heard the crack of anti-aircraft fire, apparently aiming at similar positions at the foot of the mountains.
Travellers say the road ahead has been cut for several kilometres (miles) by anti-Taleban fighters.
While this is not the frontline, it appears Taleban control of much of the road and surrounding countryside has been lost, if only for the moment.
The fighters themselves, many of them barely out of their teens, say they are confident despite the apparent setbacks.
"We are not concerned about anything. We would like to wipe out all the oppressors from here," said one 20-year-old Pushtun from the north of Afghanistan.

Most sport straggly wisps of beard, earnest expressions and the headdress and cloaks of traditional Afghanis, the uniform of the fiercely traditionalist Taleban who have swept the country since their formation in the south two years ago.

In the sometimes fast-moving frontline of this war, it is not clear what Friday's confusion will look like the following morning. But as dusk gently falls, another column of white-flagged tanks makes its way out of Kabul.
War, Afghan-style, rolls on.
